endorsements.quote: Clinicians should disclose when AI is used (eg, AI-scribed summaries, patient-portal messages, and patient education materials) to uphold patient autonomy and informed consent [ 26 ].

Crucially, policies must explicitly delineate accountability boundaries among supervising clinicians, health care institutions, and AI developers and vendors, particularly for autonomous or semiautonomous agentic workflows.

To mitigate this risk, organizations should integrate automation-off scenarios into simulation training and downtime contingency plans to ensure clinicians remain capable of detecting errors and safely resuming control.

This requires establishing governance infrastructure—such as AI steering committees and ethics review boards—to specify authorized use cases, roles and responsibilities, liability frameworks, and compliance protocols.

Accordingly, operationalized procedures and performance thresholds should be periodically reassessed—particularly following material model updates—to sustain regulatory compliance and clinical relevance.
Leaders must specify minimum performance thresholds and mandate shadow deployment phases to validate safety before full patient exposure [ 33 , 34 ].

Institutions are responsible for resourcing and coordinating these training activities, ensuring that individual clinicians are not expected to acquire advanced competencies (tiers 2 and 3) without appropriate organizational support and protected time.

unlisted_practices: Integrate AI competency training for clinicians into existing continuing medical education programs and role-specific job descriptions.
Define observable, measurable behavioral indicators to assess clinician AI competencies.
Tier AI competency requirements so that foundational skills are required of all clinicians and advanced skills of clinician leaders in governance roles.
Have clinicians verify LLM outputs against the EHR, structured data, and established clinical evidence to detect hallucinations, omissions, and misstatements.
Have clinicians avoid entering protected health information into nonintegrated or open-access LLM tools.
Have clinicians assess LLM outputs for cultural safety, linguistic accuracy, and Anglocentric bias.
Conduct equity audits of AI model performance across subgroups before deciding deployment is safe.
Require rigorous external validation, including multicenter, temporal, and geographic shift tests, before production deployment of adapted models.
Define clinician-supervised agentic AI with bounded autonomy, least-privilege permissions, audit logging, and termination and escalation criteria.
Establish rollback or pause-and-revert-to-manual protocols for deployed AI agents when performance falls below prevalidated thresholds.

screen.reason: The paper proposes a conceptual 3-tier competency and governance framework for clinicians using LLMs and AI agents, rather than presenting an empirical study.
